title: Shutdown hands rooms back while bot and AFK timers keep playing and persisting
problem: `beginShutdown()` (`shutdown.ts:74`) only sets a flag. The flag is read by the rejoin, the orphan sweep, the router and the lobby grace (`tableHandlers.ts:661,813,819`, `tableRouter.ts:294`, `socketTable.ts:248`, `socketPresence.ts:196`). It is never read by the turn timers.
proposed: Stop all turn timers in the shutdown path before `closeOwnership()`. One option is to call `clearRoomTimers(roomId)` for every `activeGames` key inside `beginShutdown()`. Alternatively, make `arm()` in `gameTimers.ts` refuse while `isShuttingDown()`.
effect: One owner per row holds through a deploy. Add a test that fires a bot timer after `beginShutdown` and asserts no write.

verify.evidence: server/http/shutdown.ts:74-86 runs beginShutdown, socketAdapterReady, io.close, settleDisconnects, then closeOwnership (drops every lock) while activeGames still holds the games. server/game/gameTimers.ts arm() (line ~58) and gameTurn.ts runBotTurn/startAfkTimer never read isShuttingDown (it is read only at tableHandlers.ts:661,813,819, tableRouter.ts:294, socketTable.ts:248, socketPresence.ts:196). A bot timer firing after closeOwnership runs commitMove -> persistGameState (gamePersistence.ts:106-125 area, writeActiveGame has no ownsRoom check; ownsRoom is read only at tableRouter.ts:133) and, on a round end, handleRoundOver's stats/rating/replay writes.
verify.correction: Reachable in production but narrow. Before closeOwnership the instance is still the legitimate lock holder, so bot moves there are harmless. The hazard window is closeOwnership to exit(0). In the healthy path drainPool (store/drainPool.ts:31-49) returns after 50 ms of quiet, so that window is usually well under the 1.2 s bot delay; it widens only when writes are in flight. The harm needs another instance to claim the freed lock and rehydrate in that window, then the old process to write a stale row (or double-write a round result if the round ends in the window). Cloud Run runs two revisions during every deploy (ADR-0003), and sockets dropped by io.close reconnect to the other revision within roughly 0.5-1.5 s, so it is possible but a few-ms-to-1-s race. The title's 'keep playing' is accurate; 'AFK' timers are slower (TURN_TIMEOUT) and are the less likely to land in the window.
verify.priority_ok: P2: narrow race window, requires a rehydrate by another instance plus a timer inside the tail; not a routine data-loss path
verify.fix_ok: Partly. Option A (clearRoomTimers for every activeGames key inside beginShutdown) is insufficient: it clears only afk/bot/autoStart (gameTimers.ts clearRoomTimers), not the per-user 'disconnect' timers, and an in-flight move handled after beginShutdown re-arms via armAfterMove. Option B (arm() refuses while shutting down) is the sound one, but isShuttingDown lives in gameRoom.ts and the flag has no reset (gameRoom.ts:148-162, tests/server/shutdownSeatLost.test.ts:1 notes it cannot be undone), so any test that arms timers after beginShutdown in the same process is poisoned; keep the guard on the timer-fire side (runBotTurn/afk callbacks return early) or inject it. Also the test should cover the closeOwnership-to-exit window, not just 'after beginShutdown'.

title: Lobby grace lives in one process, so a player who reconnects to another instance loses the seat
problem: ADR-0003 makes multi-instance real, but lobby grace is a per-process timer. Suppose a player drops on instance A and reconnects within the grace window through instance B. A's expiry asks A's own `userSocketMap`, which does not hold the player.
proposed: Make the expiry ask the cluster instead of its own maps. `isUserAtTable(userId, roomId)` already exists in `socketRegistry.ts:61` and uses `io.in(userRoom).fetchSockets()`. Then `if (await isUserAtTable(userId, roomId)) return;` replaces the local check.
effect: Removes a cross-instance seat-loss class. Deletes the false comment.
notes: ADR-0003 makes multi-instance load-bearing, so a per-process grace is a real cross-instance defect.

verify.evidence: server/socket/socketTable.ts:249-267: armLobbyGrace arms a per-process 'lobbyGrace' timer; on expiry it reads only the local userSocketMap/socketRoomMap (liveSocket && socketRoomMap.get(liveSocket) === roomId), then handleSeatRelease. A lobby (no game, so no owner) disconnect arms the grace on whichever instance saw the drop (socketPresence.ts:196-215). A reconnect on another instance goes through room:rejoin (socketRooms.ts:108-131) whose clearLobbyGrace(room.id, userId) at :129 is a local no-op there, so instance A's expiry releases a seat the player holds live on B. isUserAtTable (socketRegistry.ts:58-67) is cluster-wide and exists.
verify.correction: Scope is the pure waiting-lobby case. For a between-rounds table the grace is armed on the owner by seatLostAction and the reconnect's routed game:rejoin reaches the owner and clears it (tableHandlers.ts:491-495 comment), and the in-game 'disconnect' grace already asks the cluster (tableHandlers.ts:726 isUserOnline). The false comment is the one at tableHandlers.ts:491-493 only in the sense that it is true for the owner path and not for lobby graces.
verify.priority_ok: P2: lobby-only, recoverable by rejoining the room, needs a non-sticky reconnect to a different instance within 20 s. Real under ADR-0003, but not P1 data loss

notes: Closed #1597 (one move-commit path, typed validate()) may be partial progress; re-measure before cutting.

They differ by design (the comment at :359 explains playerMap must not be renumbered). The ready-gate difference is real but small: votesUnanimous (:309) is votes.size >= voterCount(game) (gameRoom.ts:202) while startMatchAction (:540-546) uses seatedIds.every(votes.has). #1597 (one move-commit path) already landed commitMove (gameTurn.ts:86-99), so 'move validation' extraction is partly done; playAction/passAction/exchangeAction are the remaining ~110 lines.

title: An ownership query error during reclaim is read as "claimed elsewhere" and drops live tables
problem: `takeLock` returns `null` when it cannot connect, but `false` when the query throws (`:149-151`). `reclaim` treats `false` as lost (`:170-173`). It deletes the room from `held` and disposes the game.
proposed: Return `null` from the `catch` so the existing `OWNERSHIP_RECLAIM_RETRY_MS` path covers it. This is a one-line change.
effect: Removes a data-loss path on DB failure. Add a unit test with a query that throws once.

verify.evidence: server/game/gameOwnership.ts:140-153: takeLock returns null when connect() fails but `return false` in the catch (:149-151) when the query throws. reclaim (:158-176) treats only null as 'unreachable, retry'; false does held.delete(roomId) and onRoomLost(roomId), which installTableHandlers wires to disposeGame(roomId, false) (tableHandlers.ts:836). The one-line change (return null in the catch) routes it through the existing OWNERSHIP_RECLAIM_RETRY_MS path (:171-176).
verify.correction: 'Drops live tables' is right; 'data loss' is overstated. disposeGame(roomId, false) keeps the active_games row, and the row is written on every move, so the next restore-mode action re-claims and rehydrates. What is lost is memory-only state (moveLog replay, spectators, armed timers, un-persisted in-flight vote state) and the table is disrupted until someone acts. claimRoom (:195-199) also treats the thrown-query false as 'owned elsewhere', which is the same misread on the claim path (fix applies there too).
verify.fix_ok: Sound. Note a persistently failing (non-connection) query would retry every second until it succeeds; that is bounded and acceptable. Add the throws-once test the entry proposes.

title: `disposeGame` releases the lock before the row delete lands
problem: `void releaseRoom(roomId)` (`:116`) runs right away, while the `active_games` delete is queued behind pending writes on `inRoomOrder` (`:117-124`). In that window, a restore-mode action such as rejoin or a rematch vote can find no owner, claim the lock and rehydrate the row it reads. That resurrects a table that was just disposed.
proposed: When `deleteRow` is set, release inside the same `inRoomOrder` chain after the delete settles: `void inRoomOrder(roomId, () => del().finally(() => releaseRoom(roomId)))`.
effect: Closes a resurrection race. `activeGames` is already empty, so nothing else waits on it.

verify.evidence: server/game/gamePersistence.ts:106-125 disposeGame: activeGames.delete, then `void releaseRoom(roomId)` immediately (:116), then the active_games delete queued on inRoomOrder (:117-124) behind any pending snapshot. A restore-mode action in between (tableRouter askClaimAndApply -> claimRoom -> rehydrateGame, tableHandlers.ts:140-142) finds the row still present and puts the game back in activeGames.
verify.correction: It is reachable on a single instance too, not just cross-instance: after activeGames.delete the router sees no game, and held still has the room until releaseRoom's microtask runs, so claimRoom (gameOwnership.ts:195) returns true and rehydrates from the not-yet-deleted row. Window is milliseconds (longer under DB stress), triggered by a rejoin or rematch vote arriving right after a dispose.
verify.priority_ok: P3: narrow ms window, outcome is a zombie table that the 24 h sweeper or next dispose clears
verify.fix_ok: No. Releasing inside the same inRoomOrder chain after the delete keeps the room in `held` during the window, so the same-instance race stays open; worse, if a resurrection happens in that window, the deferred releaseRoom then runs `held.delete` / pg_advisory_unlock for a room whose resurrected game is live in activeGames, producing an unowned live table (unclaimedRooms() at gameOwnership.ts:246-248 is exactly that state). A sound fix is a tombstone (a `disposing` set consulted by rehydrateGame / claim) or deleting the row before removing the game from memory.

title: Retention and prune deletes are unbounded under a 5 s statement timeout, and one policy has two homes
problem: Each sweep is one unbatched `DELETE ... WHERE ts < cutoff`. Once a backlog makes it exceed the 5 s `statement_timeout`, it times out on every run and never catches up.
proposed: Use one batched helper, `pruneOlderThan(table, where, batch=5000)`, as a `DELETE ... WHERE ctid IN (SELECT ctid ... LIMIT n)` loop.
effect: The sweep converges after an outage, and the handshake loses a write. `retention.ts` becomes the only home again.

verify.evidence: server/game/retention.ts:25-52 issues one unbatched `DELETE ... WHERE ts < cutoff` per table through db (pool with statement_timeout 5 s, store/db.ts:13,54); a timeout aborts the statement so a backlog larger than 5 s of deleting never shrinks. server/socket/ticket.ts:89 does an extra unbatched `DELETE FROM socket_ticket_nonces WHERE expires_at < now` on every handshake, a second home for the retention policy (retention.ts header says it is the single home).
verify.correction: Hypothetical today: it needs a multi-hundred-thousand-row backlog (the DB holds no real accounts yet, server/CLAUDE.md). pruneStaleRooms is already batched (STALE_ROOM_BATCH=500, gamePersistence.ts:60,266). The ticket.ts delete is per-connection rather than per-sweep, so it competes with the handshake under a reconnect storm.
verify.priority_ok: P3: not live, convergence only matters after a large backlog
verify.fix_ok: Sound. Moving the nonce prune into the sweep is the part with immediate value (it removes a write from every handshake); the ctid batching can wait.

title: HTTP rate limiters use the per-instance memory store
problem: No `store` is passed, so express-rate-limit keeps counts in process memory. Under ADR-0003 with N instances: the per-username login limit becomes about 10 × N attempts per window, and every deploy resets it. That matters because the comment at `routes.ts:139-149` calls this limiter what actually makes a password hard to guess.
proposed: Use a Postgres-backed store for the auth limiters only. A small `Store` over one `rate_limits(key, window_start, hits)` table using upsert is enough; the other limiters can stay in memory. Otherwise, record the N× ceiling as accepted in `server/CLAUDE.md`.
effect: The brute-force bound becomes cluster-wide and survives restarts.
notes: ADR-0003 (multi-instance) makes a per-instance memory store a real gap.

verify.evidence: server/http/rateLimit.ts:61-69 calls express-rate-limit without a `store`, so counts live in process memory; loginUsernameLimiter (routes.ts:~139-150, limit 10 per 15 min keyed by username) is per instance. ADR-0003 and deploy/runtime.json (pgConnectionsPerInstance) make multi-instance the running shape, so the effective ceiling is about 10 x instances and every deploy resets it.
verify.correction: The practical weakening is bounded by instance count (small single digits on this app) and each guess still pays a bcrypt compare, so it is a 'ceiling is N x' gap, not an open door. The comment at routes.ts:139-149 does overstate it as 'what makes a password hard to guess'.
verify.priority_ok: P3: multiplies a small ceiling by a small N; the second proposed option (record N x as accepted in server/CLAUDE.md) is a legitimate resolution
verify.fix_ok: Sound but costly for the benefit: a Postgres Store adds a write to every login attempt and fails open or closed during a DB outage, which must be chosen deliberately. The cheaper option (document the N x ceiling) covers the stated risk.

title: The connect path and the sweeper fetch every socket in the cluster
problem: Every connection, every `friend:get_online_list`, and every orphan or sweeper pass calls `io.fetchSockets()` over the whole cluster. Through the postgres adapter, that is a broadcast request whose reply holds every socket. A reconnect storm after a deploy is therefore O(N²) in sockets.
proposed: `onlineUserIds(ids)` → `io.in(ids.map(userRoom)).fetchSockets()`, and `tablePresence(roomId)` → `io.in(roomId).fetchSockets()`.
effect: The cost becomes proportional to friends or seats, not to the cluster.
notes: ADR-0003 multi-instance.

verify.evidence: server/socket/socketRegistry.ts onlineUserIds (~:99-111) and tablePresence (~:79-96) call `_io.fetchSockets()` over the whole cluster; socketPresence.ts:111 (connect path) and the friend:get_online_list handler (:66-77) call onlineUserIds(); gamePersistence.ts:331 (sweepFinishedTables) and tableHandlers.ts:812-826 (resumeOrphanedTables) call the same. Through the postgres adapter every call is a broadcast request whose replies carry every socket, so a reconnect storm costs O(connections x sockets).
verify.correction: isUserOnline and isUserAtTable already scope to `io.in(userRoom(userId))` (socketRegistry.ts:48-67). The cost only matters at scale; the app is not live yet.
verify.priority_ok: P3: scale-only, not live
verify.fix_ok: Mostly. onlineUserIds(ids) -> io.in(ids.map(userRoom)).fetchSockets() is sound. The tablePresence rewrite as io.in(roomId).fetchSockets() is not: rehydrateGame uses presence.online (tableHandlers.ts:~187) for players who are online but not yet in the room (mid-round case), which io.in(roomId) cannot see; it needs io.in([roomId, ...seatUserRooms]) instead.

title: Mutate→broadcast→persist→arm is repeated, and the `RoundOverWriters` seam is bypassed
problem: Ordering is documented as load-bearing: settle before serving (`gamePersistence.ts:217-219`), persist before dispose (`roundOver.ts:170-174`). Yet the sequence is open-coded at each site. The one injected seam leaks, so a test with fake writers still hits Postgres.

The true persist-before-dispose ordering is roundOver.ts:170-174. The count 'about 6 open-coded sequences / 3 close-table copies' is plausible but not checked line by line; commitMove and dealRound are the clear ones.
verify.priority_ok: P3: test-seam consistency, no defect

title: Outbound HTTP has no timeout
problem: `fetch` to the mail provider and to Expo push has no `signal`, so a hung remote holds the request, or the un-awaited invite push, forever. `mail.ts:101-104` cites the Replit "Run button", which has been stale since ADR-0006.
proposed: Add `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)` to both, and delete the stale sentence.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/http/mail.ts:75 `await fetch("https://api.resend.com/emails", {...})` and server/socket/push.ts:109 `await fetch(EXPO_PUSH_URL, {...})` pass no `signal`; grep for AbortSignal/`signal:` in server finds nothing. The CLAUDE.md-Run-button comment near mail.ts:100-104 refers to a launch path that ADR-0006 retired.

Whether the request is held depends on whether the route awaits sendMail; push is the un-awaited invite path.

title: The shutdown budget leaves out steps it spends time on
problem: `FORCED_EXIT_MS = 1500 + 6000 + 2000` counts the settle, the drain and slack. It omits `socketAdapterReady(1_000)`, `io.close()`, `closeOwnership()` and `adapterPool.end()`. Only about 1 s of the 2 s slack is really free, and the test checks just the drain against the watchdog.
proposed: Derive `FORCED_EXIT_MS` from a named list of step budgets, and have the test sum that list.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/http/shutdown.ts:34 `FORCED_EXIT_MS = DISCONNECT_SETTLE_MS + DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS + 2_000` = 1500 + 6000 + 2000 = 9500 ms. The sequence at :74-102 also spends up to 1000 ms in socketAdapterReady(1_000), plus io.close(), closeOwnership() and adapterPool.end(), none of which has a named budget. tests/server/shutdownBudget.test.ts checks only DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS > QUERY_TIMEOUT_MS, FORCED_EXIT_MS > DRAIN_TIMEOUT_MS and FORCED_EXIT_MS < sigtermGraceMs (10000).
verify.correction: 'About 1 s of the 2 s slack is free' is an estimate: the worst case (adapterReady 1 s + settle 1.5 s + drain 6 s = 8.5 s) leaves ~1 s for io.close/closeOwnership/adapter end. Every step is bounded only on its failure path; in the healthy path the whole sequence finishes in well under a second, so the watchdog (exit 1 instead of 0) only fires in a degraded shutdown.

title: The deal waits on a best-effort status write
problem: `await roomStore.updateRoomStatus(...).catch(warn)` sits before `broadcastGameState`. The write is explicitly optional, yet under DB stress it delays the deal by up to the connection wait plus the query timeout.
proposed: Make it `void` (fire-and-forget), or move it after the emits.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/game/dealRound.ts:40-44 `await roomStore.updateRoomStatus(game.roomId, "in_progress").catch(warn)` precedes broadcastGameState (:46). On the startMatch path closeForStart already set status in_progress in a transaction (roomStore.ts:150-155), so the write there is redundant; on the rematch path (tableHandlers.ts:394) it flips the status from the previous round's 'finished' back.
verify.correction: Under DB stress the delay is up to connectionTimeoutMillis (5 s, db.ts:50) plus the 5 s query timeout. Making it fire-and-forget is safe for the in-match window because joins require status 'waiting' (lobbyIntents.ts:75, roomStore claim), so a briefly stale 'finished' only refuses joins.

title: The error recorder amplifies DB outages, and client crashes inflate server errors
problem: Each error-level log line runs one `INSERT server_errors`. During a DB outage, every failed query logs an error, and each log asks for another pool checkout. That deepens the pool starvation it is reporting.
proposed: Have the recorder drop inserts while the pool has waiters, or keep a small in-memory ring and flush it from the sweeper. Log client crashes at warn level. Give bug reports their own limiter instance.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/http/serverErrors.ts:12-20 inserts one server_errors row per error-level log line through the shared app pool (db), and logger.ts tapErrors (:~58-70) calls the recorder for every line at level >= 50; a failed insert writes to stderr only, so it does not recurse but does take a pool checkout per failing line. routes.ts:~975-985 logs `logger.error(..."Client reported an unhandled error")`, so each client crash also becomes a server_errors row. errorReportLimiter (routes.ts:300-310) is keyed per session and is the limiter on the client-errors route.
verify.correction: Amplification is bounded by the 5 s query timeout and by the pool's existing waiters; it is a mild contributor, not a runaway. Bug reports sharing errorReportLimiter is plausible but not verified here.
verify.fix_ok: Logging client crashes at warn removes the inflation cleanly. Dropping inserts while the pool has waiters is sound (pool.waitingCount is available, as drainPool already reads it).

title: `/admin` and the circle leaderboard saturate the 10-connection pool
problem: `adminSnapshot` runs 18 queries in parallel against a pool of 10. The error-group queries are GROUP BYs over the whole table, despite the claim at `admin.ts:8` that "Every query is bounded". `symbolicate` parses a source map per crash group on the game process's event loop.
proposed: Bound the error groups with a date window. Run the admin queries in chunks of at most 4. Replace the per-member `currentRow` with one `inArray` query.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/http/admin.ts:235-254 starts 18 queries in one Promise.all against a pool whose default max is 10 (store/db.ts DEFAULT_POOL_MAX=10, :23); recentClientErrorGroups (clientErrors.ts:83-101) and recentServerErrorGroups (serverErrors.ts:29-37) GROUP BY the whole table with no date window, contradicting the header claim at admin.ts:8 only if 'bounded by an aggregate' is read narrowly (the comment's own definition allows aggregates). ratings.ts:224-236 getCircleLeaderboard runs currentRow once per member. sourceMaps.ts:69-89 symbolicate parses the map with SourceMapConsumer per crash group (up to ROW_LIMIT=30) on the event loop.
verify.correction: Admin-only and rare; the pool queues rather than fails (connectionTimeoutMillis 5 s). The per-member currentRow is bounded by circle size.
verify.priority_ok: P3 is right; arguably P4 given admin-only use

title: Boot DDL runs without a lock while another revision serves
problem: `ensureSchema` runs about 100 `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` statements on every boot. Postgres takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the table even when the column exists.
proposed: Wrap the DDL in `pg_advisory_xact_lock(<const>)` with `SET LOCAL lock_timeout` and a retry, or skip `ALTER`s whose column is already in `information_schema`.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/store/schemaDdl.ts:364-369 emits `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` for every column of every table on every boot, and ensureSchema (:489-496) runs them sequentially through the app pool with no lock_timeout or advisory lock (grep for advisory/lock_timeout finds none). Postgres takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on the table before noticing the column exists.
verify.correction: The count is larger than 'about 100': it is one statement per column across all tables (a few hundred). Because the app pool has a 5 s statement_timeout (db.ts:54), a boot that queues behind a long reader fails with a statement timeout and the server refuses to start (rethrown, :489 doc), while it also stalls queries queued behind it on that table. An advisory lock would only serialise concurrent boots, not remove this lock; skipping ALTERs for existing columns (information_schema or a single catalog read) is the change that removes the hazard.
verify.fix_ok: Use the second option (skip existing columns); the pg_advisory_xact_lock option does not address the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE cost. Stays additive and idempotent per server/CLAUDE.md, and tests/server/schemaDdl.test.ts would need to cover the skip.

title: `pruneStaleRooms` only knows about this process's games
problem: Candidates are filtered with the local `activeGames.has(id)` only. A room older than `STALE_ROOM_MAX_AGE_MS` that is live on another instance loses its `room_players` and `active_games` rows underneath that instance. The comment at `:290` claims a safety it only has on a single instance.
proposed: Exclude rooms with `status = 'in_progress'` or an `active_games.updated_at` within the window in SQL. That makes the guard cluster-wide.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.
notes: ADR-0003 multi-instance.

verify.evidence: server/game/gamePersistence.ts:266 `candidates.map(r => r.id).filter((id) => !activeGames.has(id))` is the only liveness guard; the doc at :251-257 says 'A room still in the in-memory map is never a candidate, whatever its age', true only for this process. Candidates are chosen by rooms.createdAt < 24 h (:258-263) and then room_players, active_games and rooms rows are deleted (:268-279).
verify.correction: Reachability is rare: it needs a room created more than 24 h ago that is still live on a different instance, i.e. a standing table running across a day (CONTEXT/GAME-RULES describe a table lasting until it breaks up), or a finished table held by connected players for a day. pruneAbandonedGames (:225-237) already uses updated_at and is cluster-safe.
verify.fix_ok: Sound: excluding rows with a recent active_games.updated_at (written on every move) makes the guard cluster-wide; waiting lobbies have no active_games row and are covered by the age check.

title: An uncaught exception exits without draining queued persists
problem: `process.exit(1)` runs immediately, which drops every write queued on `inRoomOrder` and leaves the ownership locks to time out with the connection. The comment at `:275-277` defends exiting, not exiting without the drain.
proposed: Call the existing `shutdown("uncaughtException", ...)` with a short watchdog, then exit with code 1.
effect: Not stated separately by the source.

verify.evidence: server/socket/socketSafety.ts:265-280: the uncaughtException handler logs fatal, flushes the logger and calls process.exit(1) immediately; nothing waits for roomWriteTails (gamePersistence.ts inRoomOrder) or releases locks (the ownership connection dies with the process). The comment (:274-277) argues for unconditional exit, not for skipping the drain.
verify.correction: The loss is small: persistGameState writes on every move, so only the writes queued in the last few milliseconds (and fire-and-forget stats/rating rows of a round that just ended) are dropped; locks are released by the TCP close within moments.
verify.priority_ok: P3 is generous: low value relative to risk
verify.conflict: socketSafety.ts:275-277: "Exiting is unconditional either way — a guard that could be skipped by a transport that never flushed would be no guard." and CLAUDE.md 'No self-defeating safeguards'. A drain-then-exit path that can hang on a bad process is the shape this rule warns about.
verify.fix_ok: Questionable. shutdown() runs io.close/pool drain on a process in an unknown state, ends with exit(0) on success (shutdown.ts:101) rather than 1 unless the exit hook is injected, and (see L-022) leaves game timers running while it drains, so it can write more state from the broken process. If done, it must keep a short unconditional watchdog and pass exit: () => process.exit(1).
